program_plain: World: a 64x64 lattice of cells (wrap-around edges, 8 neighbours each). Cells have 2 types (random start). Rules each step: pick a random pair of neighbouring cells; if they have the same type, all of the pair's other neighbours adopt that type.
standard_name: Sznajd model (United we stand, divided we fall), 2D square lattice with Moore neighbourhood; multi-state version for 3 types
citations: Sznajd-Weron & Sznajd 2000, Int. J. Mod. Phys. C 11(6):1157-1165 - original Sznajd model; closed community evolves to dictatorship or stalemate
Stauffer, Sousa & de Oliveira 2000, Int. J. Mod. Phys. C 12:1239-1245 - generalization to square lattice (seen only in reference lists)
Sznajd-Weron 2005, arXiv physics/0503239 'Sznajd model and its applications' - review
Stauffer 2002, Comput. Phys. Commun. 146:93-98 'Sociophysics: the Sznajd model and its applications' - review
Schulze 2004, arXiv cond-mat/0402397 - Sznajd on square lattice with more than two opinions (3 reach consensus in about half of samples)
Generalized Sznajd model for opinion propagation (ResearchGate listing) - simulations with 2-6 opinions on square lattice, finite-size consensus/coexistence
searches: Sznajd model opinion evolution in closed community Sznajd-Weron 2000
Sznajd model review Sociophysics two-dimensional square lattice consensus multi-state opinions
notes: Moore-neighbourhood pair selection (diagonal pairs allowed) differs slightly from the usual von Neumann pair or plaquette, which is unlikely to matter. full_text:
**Verdict: KNOWN.** This is the Sznajd model ("United we stand, divided we fall") on a square lattice, with a Moore-neighbourhood pair-selection variant.

**1. Model family.** This is opinion dynamics, a sociophysics Ising/Potts-like model. A random neighbouring pair that agrees convinces its surrounding neighbours. The 3-type variant is the multi-opinion Sznajd model.

**2. The specific behaviour.** Your three observations are:
- **One type fills most of the lattice.** The literature describes this as consensus, or "dictatorship". The original paper reports that a closed community has to evolve either to a dictatorship or a stalemate state. A later paper calls the stationary states always consensus states.
- **Rising activity.** This is probably the density of agreeing pairs, which can trigger updates. It rises as ordered domains coarsen. I did not find a source that reports this quantity directly, so I am inferring it from the mechanism. The mechanism is that updates only fire on agreeing pairs, and each update creates more agreeing pairs.
- **Spatial clustering (high Moran's I).** This is the domain coarsening that precedes consensus. I did not find a source that reports Moran's I specifically. Domain formation follows from the same mechanism.

**3. Earliest source and reviews.**
- **Earliest source:** Sznajd-Weron & Sznajd, "Opinion evolution in closed community", Int. J. Mod. Phys. C 11(6), 1157–1165 (2000). I checked the title, authors, year and venue in the ADS and RePEc records. It was a 1D chain model. It found a power law in the decision time distribution.
- **Two-dimensional generalisation:** Stauffer, Sousa & de Oliveira, "Generalization to square lattice of Sznajd sociophysics model", Int. J. Mod. Phys. C 12, 1239–1245 (2000). I only saw this in a reference list, so title, authors and venue are confirmed from the list but not the content. A related Stauffer paper says that, on the square lattice, a pair (or plaquette) of neighbours convinces its six (eight) nearest neighbours when all members agree.
- **Reviews:**
  - Sznajd-Weron, "Sznajd model and its applications" (arXiv physics/0503239). It reviews modifications and applications, and says the model differs from voter or Ising-type models because information flows outward.
  - Stauffer, "Sociophysics: the Sznajd model and its applications", Comput. Phys. Commun. 146, 93–98 (2002).
- **Multi-opinion versions:** Square-lattice consensus with several opinions has been simulated. One paper reports simulations for 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 opinions in a square lattice. Another notes that with the Sznajd rule three opinions reach a consensus in roughly half of the samples, and four only rarely. That paper is a global-local variant, so this is indirect support for the 3-type case. Another overview says it was adapted to deal with more than two opinions in networks of different topologies in 2002.
- **Finite-size and coexistence effects:** On finite lattices, finite size effects cause a transition with the length of the relaxation period between coexistence and consensus. With 3 types on a 64×64 lattice, expect slow or incomplete consensus in some runs.

**Differences from the canonical model.** These are minor and unlikely to change the behaviour:
- **Pair selection:** the 8-neighbour (Moore) lattice allows diagonal pairs. Stauffer's version used von Neumann pairs, or 2×2 plaquettes with eight neighbours.
- **Updating:** this system uses random sequential updating. Stauffer's work finds that simultaneous updating changes the behaviour, but random sequential updating is the standard setting.

**5. Confidence: high.** The rule is exactly the Sznajd rule on a square lattice, and consensus and coarsening under it are well documented. The caveats are that I could not read the full texts of the older papers, and that the "activity" and Moran's I readouts are not named in any source I found.
